newsitem.title: DUBAI: Riyad Bank says coordinating SABIC loan.
newsitem.headline: Riyad Bank says coordinating SABIC loan.

text.p: Riyadh Bank said on Wednesday it was coordinating a $850 million syndicated loan mandated by industrial and petrochemical giant Saudi Basic Industries Corp (SABIC) for one of its affiliates.

The Saudi Arabian bank said in a statement the loan, from local, regional and international banks, would "provide the commercial term debt required" to finance the construction of a petrochemical complex by the Industrial Fibres Company (Ibn Rushd), owned by SABIC as well as Saudi and Bahraini firms.
The complex of several petrochemical projects, including a polyester plant which started production in October 1995, will cost up to $1.9 billion.

It named the banks as Riyad Bank, the Riyadh-based Arab National Bank -- owned by Amman-based Arab Bank and Saudi investors -- Bahrain-based Gulf International Bank, JP Morgan, Britain's Barclays Bank Plc, Industrial Bank of Japan, the Arab Petroleum Investments Corp (APICORP) and Saudi Cairo Bank.
A SABIC statement issued earlier in the day said the deal was signed on November 12.

"The project enjoys strong support from SABIC and other shareholders as evidenced by the high equity contribution and their commitment to complete the project, in addition to support from the Saudi Industrial Development Fand (SIDF)," said the Riyad Bank statement faxed to Reuters.
"Ibn Rushd has received strong financing interest from both regional and international banks," it added.

Bankers in the Gulf this week told Reuters the eight banks -- who are equal arrangers -- had received the mandate earlier in the month and had been waiting for a final word from Ibn Rushd before starting preparations for the syndication.
They said the consortium will approach regional and international banks to take part in the syndication and did not foresee any problems in raising the loan.

SABIC said Ibn Rushd will use the loan to finance the construction of a 350,000-tonnes per year purified terephthalic acid (PTA) plant -- due to come on stream in 1997 -- as well as a world-scale aromatic plant -- which would produce 350,000 metric tonnes of benzene and 300,000 metric tonnes of paraxylene a year. It will also produce orthoxylene and metaxylene and is due to come on stream by early 1998.

Saudi Arabia is expanding and opening up its petrochemical sector to private finance in an attempt to diversify its oil-dominated economy. New multi-million dollar petrochemical plants feeding off the country's abundant gas reserves are expected to come on stream until early into the next decade.
